en: 125(27.3) *The Sūtra on Sudatta* Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavidi of Central India during the Qi Dynasty.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the householder Sudatta went to where the World-Honored One was; having arrived, he prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and withdrew to sit to one side.
Once the householder Sudatta had sat down to one side, the World-Honored One addressed him, saying:
"Is it so, householder?
Do you give alms while living at home?"
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
Among those who give as householders, there are gifts that are not of fine food; some offer a soup made of mixed coarse grains and hemp seeds, with a single piece of ginger as the gift.”
“Householder, this is not a sublime gift. As for a sublime gift,
both [the giver and the recipient] receive its fruit.”
"Householder!

You are one who gives an unexcellent gift; you give without faith, you do not give at the proper time, you do not give with your own hands, nor do you go to meet the recipient to give. You give without knowledge and without faith, and you give without knowing that there is a result."

One should know that such is the retribution: the mind is not set upon magnificent dwellings, nor is it set upon various exquisite objects, nor is it set upon clothing and bedding, nor is it set upon exquisite food, nor is it set upon the five exquisite sensual pleasures of lust.
Why is this? Householder!
Because he practices what is not the fruit of giving.
Householder!

One who practices what is not [merely] giving should possess faith; they should give at the proper time, give with their own hands, and go forth to give. Possessing knowledge and faith, they give having understood the causal conditions of retribution.

One should know that when such a retribution exists for him, his mind becomes intent upon excellent household affairs; he possesses extremely exquisite utensils, extremely exquisite clothing, and has extremely exquisite food, and his mind indulges in the five exquisite sensual pleasures.
For what reason?
Householder,
you should know that he possesses giving.
"Householder!

You practice sublime giving, yet you give without faith, you do not give at the proper time, you do not give with your own hand, you do not go to the recipient to give, and you neither know nor believe [in the Dharma]. Furthermore, you practice giving without knowing that there are causes and conditions for the ripening of karmic fruit."

You should know that such a person receives this retribution; their mind is not set upon excellent family affairs, nor is it set upon fine clothing, nor is it set upon delicious food, nor is it set upon the five exquisite sensual pleasures.
Why is this? Householder!
This is not because it is a gift.

"Householder! One who gives excellently gives with faith and joy; gives at the appropriate time; gives with their own hands; goes in person to give; gives with understanding and conviction; and gives having understood that there are results and fruits for one's actions."
You should know that such is the retribution he receives: his mind is set upon the affairs of a noble household, and his mind is set upon the five exquisite sensual pleasures and food.
Why is this so? O householder!
One should thus give gifts according to the occasion.
Why is this? Householder!

In a past age, there was a great brahmin named Velaṇa, who was immensely wealthy and possessed vast riches and diverse goods. He performed such great acts of giving that he filled eighty-four thousand golden bowls with crushed silver;
he performed such great acts of giving that he filled eighty-four thousand silver bowls with crushed gold;
and he performed such great acts of giving that he offered eighty-four thousand elephants, all magnificently adorned and white as snow.
He practiced such great giving by offering eighty-four thousand horses, all adorned with golden necklaces;
he practiced such great giving by offering eighty-four thousand oxen, each tied with garments and yielding milk that constantly filled their milking vessels;
he practiced such great giving by offering eighty-four thousand precious women, beautiful and exquisite, all most magnificently adorned with every kind of ornament.
Thus one performs such great giving, yet other foods and various flavors remain beyond counting.

That is to say, if a wealthy householder, such as the very rich Brahmin Velaṃba, were to perform such great giving by bestowing it upon the ordinary persons of Jambudvīpa, it would be better to give it to a single seer (ṛṣi), for that would yield greater merit.

Although the householder Vimala, the wealthy brahmin, made such a great offering by giving it to the seers of Jambudvīpa, it does not equal the merit obtained from giving to a single srotāpanna; the latter gains far more merit.

Even if that wealthy householder, the great Brahmin Vairaṇa, were to give to all the ordinary persons, sages, and one hundred stream-enterers (srotāpanna) in Jambudvīpa, it would not equal the merit gained by giving to a single once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin); the latter would obtain far more merit.

Although a wealthy householder or a great brahmin such as Velaṇa might give such gifts to the ordinary people, sages, one hundred stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*), and one hundred once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*) of Jambudvīpa, it would not equal the merit obtained by giving to a single non-returner (*anāgāmin*); this latter gift yields far more merit.

Although a wealthy householder or a great Brahmin such as Vimala might give such gifts to ordinary persons throughout Jambudvīpa up to a hundred Anāgāmins, it would not equal the merit obtained by giving to a single Arhat; the latter gains far more merit.

Householder, although the great and wealthy Brahmin Vimala might give such gifts to all the ordinary persons and up to a hundred Arhats in Jambudvīpa, it would not equal the merit obtained by giving to a single Pratyekabuddha; the latter yields far more merit.

"Householder, although the great wealthy Brahmin Vimala makes such a gift, giving it to ordinary persons throughout Jambudvīpa up to a hundred pratyekabuddhas, it does not equal the merit obtained by giving to a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; this latter gift yields far more merit."

It is said that if a householder or a wealthy Brahmin such as Vimala were to give such gifts—giving to ordinary persons throughout Jambudvīpa up to as many as a hundred pratyekabuddhas—and were instead to build a dwelling to offer to the Saṃgha of the four quarters, he would obtain much greater merit.

Householder, suppose a wealthy Brahmin such as Velaṇa were to give such gifts as these—giving to the ordinary people of Jambudvīpa, up to the point of building dwellings and giving them to the Saṃgha of the four quarters—it would not equal the merit obtained by one who, with a pure mind, takes the three refuges in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Bhikṣu-saṃgha, and receives their precepts; this latter obtains much more merit.

Householder, even if a wealthy Brahmin such as Vela were to perform such a great act of giving—bestowing gifts upon the ordinary people of Jambudvīpa and leading them to take the three refuges in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha with pure conduct and receive their precepts—it would not equal the merit gained by practicing loving-kindness toward all sentient beings for even as long as it takes to milk a cow; the latter gains far more merit.

Householder, compared to a wealthy Brahmin such as Vairaṇa giving such gifts to ordinary people throughout Jambudvīpa, or practicing loving-kindness toward all sentient beings for as long as it takes to milk a cow;

or compared to one who contemplates and reflects that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self for even as long as a finger-snap—this latter person gains far more merit.
"You, householder!
You should think thus:
'Is that householder Vimala, the very wealthy brahmin, someone else?'"
"Do not think thus: 'I am that very person named the wealthy Brahmin Velaṇa! It is so, householder!

Abiding in one's own welfare and the welfare of others, for the benefit of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the sake of the well-being, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans, I have taught the Dharma in this way; yet it was not ultimate, not stainless, not the ultimate holy life, and I had not practiced the holy life to its conclusion. Therefore, one is not yet liberated from birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, and dissatisfaction; I say such a person is not yet liberated from suffering."
"Householder!

Now the Tathāgata has appeared in the world—the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One. For his own sake, for the sake of others, for the sake of many people, and out of compassion for the world, he brings benefit, happiness, and peace to gods and humans."

I now preach the Dharma for you—ultimate exhaustion, ultimate stainlessness, the ultimate holy life, and the ultimate practice of the holy life; having now attained liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, and suffering, I declare that one is already free from suffering.
Thus the Buddha spoke.
Having heard what the World-Honored One had said, the householder Sudatta rejoiced and was filled with joy.
The Sūtra on Sudatta Spoken by the Buddha.
